title: The Complexity Kink: LLM Rubric Instruments for Causal Inference on Code Generation Reliability
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: Complexity measured from generated output is confounded by failure: pass rate varies non-monotonically with output complexity, and many failures are short outputs from hard prompts.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, line plot beside 2x2 heatmap with outlined cell
description: Two panels. Panel (a), "Output-side reliability curve", is a dual-axis line plot. A bold red line with markers and a light shaded band shows mean pass rate (left axis, 0.65 to 0.95) against Lizard cyclomatic complexity of the generated output (x axis, 1 to 40). The red line dips to about 0.74 near CC 12 and then climbs to a peak near CC 26. A dashed blue line shows mean prompt rubric composite on the right axis and rises from about 4 to 15. Panel (b), "Failed complete cases (outcome 0)", is a 2x2 blue heatmap. Rows are prompt index at most 8 or above 8. Columns are output CC at most 10 or above 10. Cells show counts and percentages. The lower-left cell, 3,561 (25.0%), has a red outline and a "reverse-threshold cell" label. The darkest cell, lower-right, draws the eye along with the red outline.
caption: Generated-output complexity is failure-dependent. (a) Across 103,948 complete-case generations, points show mean pass rate by integer Lizard output CC; the shaded descriptive band is ±1.96 generation-row standard errors and does not adjust for repeated prompts or models. Here 40 denotes CC ≥40. The dashed blue line is the conditional mean prompt composite, read on the right axis. (b) Among failed complete cases (outcome 0), the outlined cell contains 3,561 of 14,247 generations (25.0%): the prompt composite is > 8 while generated-output CC is ≤10.
abstract: Measuring complexity from a model's own code is biased by failure: a hard prompt can produce a short, broken program that looks simple. We instead score each prompt's structure on six dimensions from the prompt alone, never from generated code or test results. We draw 5,000 Python prompts across six bands of a preliminary single-rater score, and four out-of-panel LLM judges rescore every prompt (19,997 scores; composite ICC(2,1) = 0.872 on the 4,998 prompts with all four). Twenty-one models answer every prompt (105,000 generations), and an independent LLM auditor, checked against known-answer cases, reviews each unit-test verdict. Averaged over models, pass rate has a nonmonotone breakpoint at composite $\hat{\gamma}=14.0$: 83.4\% at or below, 90.1\% above. That jump is not a law of difficulty. With task-type fixed effects the breakpoint stays at 14.0 but the adjusted jump shrinks from 6.8 to 0.4 points, and neither of the benchmark's two prompt sources reproduces the jump on its own. Nineteen models pass more often above their own breakpoint and two less often, and one of those two declines, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview's, comes from 156 API calls that returned nothing. In post hoc follow-up, Kimi K2.5 shows the clearest decline: with a prompt-source control, and within the later source alone, its break is at 14.25, where its later-source pass rate falls from 0.848 to 0.808 (95\% interval $[14.00,14.75]$). A 365-prompt audit-clean extension matches the original raw test outcomes at bins 15 and 16 but adds only 14 prompts above bin 16. Among failed generations with measurable output complexity, 25.0\% pair a prompt composite above 8 with output complexity of at most 10, twice the share among passing ones. The pooled breakpoint moves to 11.25 on raw test outcomes and 13.75 under the partial audit used at submission. Human agreement with the index is moderate and rater-dependent, paraphrase and cross-language rescoring preserve its ordering, and overidentification tests reject the six dimensions as instruments, so we treat the composite as an index and make no causal claim. The contribution is a prompt-side way to locate where each model's pass rate changes and to test how much that depends on the prompt mix and on how success is scored.
